rows: The house centipede has a compound eye of about 150 to 200 facets on each side of its head. Most large tropical centipedes have four simple eyes on each side, and the soil centipedes have none.
The house centipede's eye is most sensitive to blue light near 448 nanometres and has a second peak in ultraviolet near 350. This view weights its grey toward blue and leaves the ultraviolet out.
No one has measured how much detail a centipede sees. This view assumes the house centipede sees nearly three times as sharply as a millipede, because its eye has about seven times as many facets.
Centipedes run from light and toward dark shapes. The house centipede, the brown centipede and a large Scolopendra all head for a dark screen at the side of an arena.
A large Asian centipede feels sunlight as heat in its antennae, which warm by more than 8 degrees Celsius within ten seconds of strong sun.
Soil centipedes are blind. In one of them every known gene for sensing light is missing, while the house centipede keeps those genes.
With &draw=shadow, a sudden fall of light sends a dark ring across the picture. The ring is the app's drawing.
A centipede finds prey and mates largely by smell and touch through its antennae, and a camera records neither.

rows.title: Eyes
rows.text: If you are a house centipede, each of your eyes is a small triangle of about 150 tiny units, and each unit has its own cornea and a crystal cone under it; if you are a Scutigera forceps, each eye has about 200. If you belong to the order Geophilomorpha, the centipedes that live underground, you are blind. For most other centipedes, nobody has counted the eyes or described what kind they are.
rows.note: Left out R6 (four ocelli per side) because its quote says "other species" without naming the group, and R5/R7 (blind scolopendromorphs) because they do not state a count for a named species.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a house centipede, Scutigera coleoptrata, recordings from the retina of your eye found two peaks of sensitivity, one in blue light near 450 nanometers and one in ultraviolet near 350 nanometers. The researchers expect you have at least two kinds of visual pigment. Nobody has measured the color sense of any other centipede.
rows.note: Only Scutigera coleoptrata has records; the row says nothing about other Scutigera species or other orders.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see. No one has tested how much fine detail your eyes can pick out, so there is no number to compare with the 30 cycles a degree that a human reads on an eye chart.
rows.note: No records were supplied, so the row only says that acuity is unmeasured and cites nothing; I left out eye structure and any centipede-specific claim. The species list includes the centipede grass orchid (Zeuxine strateumatica), a plant, which looks like a name match by mistake.

rows.title: Smell and touch
rows.text: If you are a house centipede, your brain has well-developed centers for smell and for touch. If you are a brown centipede, one study found evidence that pores at the base of your legs release a scent that differs between males and females. Nobody has measured how faint a smell you can detect or how light a touch you can feel.
rows.note: Left out R5 (genome commentary on Strigamia, grade g) and the plant records R1, R4; no record measures touch sensitivity in any centipede.
